title: The Sun, the Moon, the stars and the planets
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers NIOS Class 3, Lesson 6 'Sun-Moon-Stars, Day-Night and Seasons' (Sun, Moon and stars; stars and planets; the Sun and its planets; day and night; seasons). No textbook needed.
summary: The Sun is a star, and every star you see at night is a sun, so far away that it looks like a dot. Your child walks a scale model of the Sun and its eight planets, makes the Moon's phases with a ball and a lamp, and finds the Saptarishi and the Pole Star. With a ball, a torch and a tilted pencil, they see what really causes day and night, the year and the seasons.
builds_on: In Class 2 (Day, night and rhythms of nature) your child tracked the Sun's walk across the sky and learned that the Earth turns. Next, in Class 4, they will keep a month-long Moon diary, read shadows like a clock and learn how the Sun lights up planets, moons and comets. In Class 5 they will draw latitude and longitude, explain time zones and learn about satellites.
goals: By the end your child can explain that the Sun is a star, and why the other stars look so small.
By the end your child can tell a star from a planet and a moon: stars make their own light; planets and moons shine with reflected sunlight.
By the end your child can name the eight planets in order from the Sun and say which are rocky and which are giants.
By the end your child can show with a ball and a lamp why the Moon seems to change shape.
By the end your child can show that the Earth's spin makes day and night, its trip round the Sun makes a year, and its tilt makes seasons.

days.title: What's up there?
days.goal: Wonder at the sky and sort what we see into stars, planets and the Moon.

steps.title: The Sun's walk, remembered
steps.do: Ask: 'In Class 2 we watched the Sun move across the sky. Where does it rise? Where does it set? Does it really move?' Good answers: 'in the east', 'in the west', 'no, the Earth turns'. If your child did not do the Class 2 rung, they turn slowly on the spot in front of a lamp to see the lamp 'rise' and 'set'.

steps.title: Everything in the sky
steps.do: Ask your child to name everything they have ever seen in the sky, by day or night. Write each on a slip of paper: Sun, Moon, stars, clouds, birds, aeroplanes, lightning, rainbow, a bright dot that does not twinkle (often a planet). Sort the slips together into 'in our air' and 'out in space'. Ask: 'Which of the space things make their own light? Why do you think so?' Leave the answer open for now.

steps.title: Story: The Firefly Who Wanted to Be a Star
steps.do: Read the story aloud. Stop when Tara the firefly reaches the top of the jamun tree and ask: 'Why do you think she came no closer to the stars?' Finish the story and ask the story questions.

steps.title: Dusk sky watch
steps.do: At dusk, go to a terrace, balcony or open ground away from bright lights. Look west, where the Sun set. Ask: 'What is the first bright dot you see?' Often it is a planet, Venus or Jupiter. A planet shines steadily, while stars twinkle. Count the stars as they appear for 5 minutes. Write what you saw on the first page of the sky book.

steps.title: Star or not?
steps.do: Ask: 'Is the Sun a star?' Accept any answer and say: 'Tomorrow we test it.'

need: a notebook for the sky book

days.title: The Sun is a star
days.goal: Find out why the Sun looks so big and the stars so small.

steps.title: Last night's sky
steps.do: Look at last night's notes. Ask: 'Did all the dots twinkle? Did any shine steadily?' Say: 'A star is so far away that its light comes from a single tiny point. Our moving air shakes that point about, so it twinkles. A planet is nearer and looks like a tiny disc, so it twinkles less.'

steps.title: Near torch, far torch
steps.do: Do Experiment e1 in a long corridor, a terrace at dusk or a dark room.

steps.title: How big is the Sun?
steps.do: Say: 'About 109 Earths would fit across the Sun, and more than a million Earths would fit inside it. It looks small only because it is about 15 crore kilometres away. A car going at 100 kilometres an hour without stopping would take about 170 years to get there.' Put a mustard seed (the Earth) next to a football (the Sun) to show the sizes. Ask: 'If the Sun is a star, what are the stars?' Good answer: 'suns, very far away'.

steps.title: Light makers and light bouncers
steps.do: In a dark room, shine a torch on a steel plate, a mirror and a dull cloth. Ask: 'Is the plate making light, or is the light bouncing off it?' Say: 'The Sun and the stars make their own light. The Moon and the planets are like the steel plate. They shine only because sunlight bounces off them. This is called reflecting light.' Add both to the sky book.

steps.title: Stars come in colours
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v4, Annie Jump Cannon, who sorted hundreds of thousands of stars by their light. Say: 'Stars are not all white. Blue-white stars are the hottest, yellow stars like our Sun are in the middle, and orange-red stars are the coolest.' On a clear winter evening, look for orange Betelgeuse and blue-white Rigel in the star pattern called Orion. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Never look at the Sun
steps.do: Ask your child to say the safety rule: never look straight at the Sun, not even with sunglasses, binoculars or a telescope.

need: a mustard seed and a football
a steel plate, a mirror and a cloth

days.title: The Sun's family
days.goal: Meet the eight planets and feel how far apart they are.

steps.title: Planet names
steps.do: Teach the order of the planets with this line: 'My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles'. The first letters stand for Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Say it together three times.

steps.title: The planet walk
steps.do: Do Activity a1, the planet walk, on a terrace, in a ground or along a quiet road. In a flat, use the smaller version in the activity.

steps.title: Rocky and giant
steps.do: Ask: 'Which planets were tiny and close together near the Sun?' (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars). Say: 'These four are rocky, with hard ground. The next four are giants, made mostly of gas and ice, with no ground to stand on. About 1,300 Earths would fit inside Jupiter.'

steps.title: Is Pluto a planet?
steps.do: Read voice v1 together. Lay out the facts: Pluto is smaller than our Moon, and many similar icy worlds have been found beyond Neptune. Ask the voice question and let your child vote, with a reason.

steps.title: Planet music
steps.do: Play two short pieces from The Planets, written for orchestra by Gustav Holst between 1914 and 1916: 'Mars, the Bringer of War' and 'Jupiter, the Bringer of Jollity'. Ask: 'Which one sounds like a giant? Why do you think so?' Say: 'Mars is named after the Roman god of war, perhaps because of its blood-red colour.' Holst wrote no piece for the Earth. Ask: 'What would the Earth's music sound like?'

need: a measuring tape or long rope
9 paper labels for the Sun and the planets
rava grains, two mustard seeds, two marbles, two chana and a football

days.title: The Moon, our companion
days.goal: Show why the Moon seems to change shape.

steps.title: Moon memories
steps.do: Ask: 'What shapes have you seen the Moon in?' Draw them: full, half, a thin curve. Ask: 'Does the Moon really change shape?' Leave it open.

steps.title: Ball-and-lamp Moon
steps.do: Say: 'The Moon is the Earth's satellite. That means it goes round the Earth, about once a month.' Then do Experiment e2 in a dark room. Your child turns with the ball and names each shape they see. Draw the four main shapes in the sky book.

steps.title: Shukla Paksha and Krishna Paksha
steps.do: Say: 'Indian calendars have followed the Moon for thousands of years. Shukla Paksha, the bright half, is the 15 days when the lit part grows, from Amavasya (new Moon) to Purnima (full Moon). Krishna Paksha, the dark half, is the 15 days when it shrinks again.' Ask: 'Which festivals fall on a full Moon or a new Moon?' (Karthigai Deepam, Chitra Pournami, Buddha Purnima and Holi fall on a full Moon. The main night of Diwali, Lakshmi Puja, is on Amavasya. Eid begins when the first thin crescent is seen.)

steps.title: Galileo looks up
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v2, Galileo, who pointed a telescope at the Moon and Jupiter in 1609 and 1610. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Draw tonight's Moon
steps.do: If the Moon is up tonight, your child draws it in the sky book and writes the date.

need: a white ball or orange on a pencil

days.title: Patterns of stars
days.goal: Find the Saptarishi and Pole Star, and learn what stars are made of.

steps.title: Join the dots
steps.do: Scatter dots on a page and ask your child to join some into a picture. Say: 'People everywhere have done this with the stars. The stars in a pattern only look close together from Earth. Many are at very different distances. The pictures were made by people, not by the stars.'

steps.title: What are stars made of?
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v3, Cecilia Payne, who found in 1925 that stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Star-pattern viewer
steps.do: Do Activity a2: make a Saptarishi star viewer with a paper cup and a pin. Shine a torch through it onto the ceiling.

steps.title: Find the Saptarishi and Dhruva Tara
steps.do: After dark, best between February and June, look north. Find the seven bright stars of the Saptarishi, shaped like a ladle (also called the Big Dipper). The two stars at the front of the ladle's bowl point to Dhruva Tara, the Pole Star. It stays almost still all night while the other stars move round it. In South India it sits low, just above the northern horizon, so you need a clear view north. Say: 'Bright lights on Earth hide the stars. More than a third of people on Earth can no longer see the Milky Way from home.'

steps.title: A star-stuff thought
steps.do: Say: 'Stars make new materials inside them. Some of the iron in your blood was made inside stars that exploded before the Sun was born.' Ask: 'What do you think about that?'

steps.title: Paint the cities of stars
steps.do: Say: 'The Milky Way is our galaxy, a huge group of more than a hundred billion stars. There are billions of other galaxies. Some are spirals like pinwheels (ours is one). Some are smooth and round or egg-shaped. Some are irregular, with no clear shape.' Your child draws one of each on black paper with white chalk, and puts a tiny dot in an arm of the spiral labelled 'we are here'.

need: a copy of the Saptarishi dot pattern

days.title: Spin and journey
days.goal: Use a ball and a lamp to see what makes day, night and a year.

steps.title: Spin or journey?
steps.do: Stand up. Spin on the spot once and say 'rotation'. Walk once round a chair and say 'revolution'. Your child does each and says its name.

steps.title: A tiny India on a ball
steps.do: Do Experiment e3. Stick a tiny paper India on a ball, shine the lamp on it, and spin the ball anticlockwise as seen from the top. Your child calls out sunrise, noon, sunset and midnight for India. Ask: 'When it is day in India, where is it night?' (on the other side of the ball, for example in the USA).

steps.title: Walk the orbit
steps.do: Put the lamp in the middle of the room. Your child holds the ball and walks slowly round the lamp in a big circle, spinning the ball as they go. Say: 'The Earth spins about 365 times while it goes round the Sun once. That is why a year has 365 days.' Ask: 'How old are you? So how many times have you gone round the Sun?'

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Your child does the core worksheet ws1. Help with reading. For the 'why' questions, they explain aloud before writing.

need: a small paper India and tape

days.title: Why are there seasons?
days.goal: Test the real reason for summer and winter.

steps.title: Hot and cold
steps.do: Ask: 'Why do you think May is hotter than January in Chennai?' Many people say 'because the Earth is nearer the Sun'. Write down your child's idea and their reason. Say: 'Let's test it.'

steps.title: Season dance
steps.do: Your child is the Earth. They hold a pencil, tilted towards one wall of the room, as their axis (the line the Earth spins around). They walk round a lamp in four steps. At each step, play music and your child dances that season: spring (arms slowly rising), summer (big and wide), monsoon (swaying, fingers pattering like rain), winter (small and curled). Ask: 'Did the pencil change which way it leaned?' (no, it always leaned towards the same wall). Say: 'Keep that in mind. It is why we have seasons, and the next test shows how.'

steps.title: Straight and slanting light
steps.do: Do Experiment e4 with a torch and squared paper. Your child counts the squares in each patch of light and says which patch would feel warmer if it were sunlight.

steps.title: The tilted Earth
steps.do: Push a pencil through the ball at a slant. Walk it round the lamp, keeping the pencil always leaning towards the same wall. Your child watches the top half of the ball. Ask: 'When is the top half leaning towards the lamp? When is it leaning away?' Say: 'When our half of the Earth leans towards the Sun, sunlight hits us more directly and the days are longer. That is summer. When it leans away, it is winter. In fact the Earth is nearest the Sun in early January, during our winter.'

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Your child does the stretch worksheet ws2. Read the questions aloud. For the two written questions, they explain aloud first, then write.

days.title: Sky book, game, check and teach it back

steps.title: Star, Planet or Moon?
steps.do: Play the card game g1 together. Each answer needs a reason, for example: 'It is a planet, because it does not make its own light.'

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Your child tries the challenge worksheet ws3. Talk through the puzzles. Praise a good reason even when the answer is wrong.

steps.title: End check
steps.do: Ask the check questions. For any muddled answer, go back to the ball and the lamp.

steps.title: Teach it back with the sky book
steps.do: Your child finishes the sky book. With the book, the ball and the lamp, they teach a family member: the Sun is a star, the planets and the Moon reflect its light, the Earth's spin makes day and night, its journey round the Sun makes a year, and its tilt makes the seasons. The listener asks one 'why' question.

the Moon goes round the Earth

it is the same as straight light

sections.p: Amavasya is the new Moon night, when we cannot see the Moon. Where is the Moon then?

Karthik is 8 years old. How many times has he travelled round the Sun? Explain.

worksheets.title: Sky puzzles

sections.p: If you lived on the Moon, what would the Earth look like? Would it have phases too?
Pluto: planet or not? Give one reason for each side, then say what you think.
After sunset you see a bright dot in the west. It is not twinkling. What is it most likely to be?
Australia is in the bottom half of the Earth. In December it is winter in India. What season does Australia have in December?

sections: B. Big numbers and the evidence

sections.p: If the Sun were a football, the Earth would be about the size of...
Stars are made mostly of hydrogen and ____.
Is each animal busy at night or in the day?
A dung beetle in Africa steers by the Milky Way at night. If city lights hide the Milky Way, what might happen to the beetle? Who should decide how bright our nights are?

experiments.title: Near torch, far torch
experiments.question: Why do stars look so small and dim if they are really suns?
need: a long corridor, terrace or field at dusk
steps: Switch both torches on. You and your child each hold one, side by side. Compare them: they look the same.
You walk 5 big steps away and point your torch at your child. Compare again.
Walk 20 steps, then as far as you can.
Each time, ask: 'Which looks bigger? Which looks brighter?'
experiments.predict: Ask: 'When I walk away, will my torch change? Will it look different?'
experiments.observe: The far torch looks smaller and dimmer, even though it is just as bright as the near one.
experiments.why: The further away a light is, the more its light spreads out before it reaches your eye. So it looks fainter and smaller. The Sun is our nearest star. The next nearest star is so far away that its light takes more than four years to reach us. That is why stars, which are suns, look like tiny dots.
experiments.safety: Don't shine a torch straight into anyone's eyes from close up.

experiments.title: Ball-and-lamp Moon
experiments.question: Why does the Moon seem to change shape?
need: a white ball or an orange stuck on a pencil
steps: Put the lamp on one side of the room. It is the Sun. Your child's head is the Earth.
Your child holds the ball (the Moon) at arm's length, a little above their head.
They turn slowly on the spot, anticlockwise, watching the ball the whole time.
Stop at four places: ball towards the lamp, ball to the left, ball away from the lamp, ball to the right. Each time, ask: 'How much of the lit side can you see?'
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will the ball always look the same? What will we see when it is between you and the lamp?'
experiments.observe: Ball towards the lamp: the lit side faces away and the ball looks dark (new Moon). Ball to one side: half lit (half Moon). Ball away from the lamp: fully lit (full Moon). In between, you see thin crescents and nearly full shapes.
experiments.why: Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun, just as half the ball is always lit by the lamp. The Moon goes round the Earth about once every 29 and a half days. As it goes, we see more or less of its lit half. The Earth's shadow does not cause the phases. It falls on the Moon only in an eclipse.
experiments.safety: Keep the lamp cord out of the way. Don't touch a hot bulb.

experiments.title: A tiny India on a ball
experiments.question: How does the spinning Earth give us day and night?
need: a tiny paper India and tape
steps: Tape the tiny India on the ball about a third of the way down from the top.
Hold the ball by the pencil in front of the lamp, which is the Sun.
Spin it slowly anticlockwise (seen from the top).
Stop when India is in the light, at the edge, in the dark, and at the other edge.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'When will India have midday? When will it be midnight?'
experiments.observe: Half the ball is always lit (day) and half dark (night). As it spins, India moves into the light (sunrise), faces the lamp (noon), moves into the dark (sunset) and is opposite the lamp (midnight).
experiments.why: The Earth spins once in about 24 hours. Only the half facing the Sun has day. The Sun does not go round us. We turn to face it, and then away again. This spin is called rotation.

experiments.title: Straight and slanting light
experiments.question: Why is sunlight weaker in winter?
steps: In a dim room, shine the torch straight down onto the squared paper from 20 cm. Draw round the spot of light and count the squares inside.
Now tilt the torch so it shines at a slant from the same distance. Draw round the patch and count the squares.
Compare how bright each patch looks.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will the slanting light make a bigger or smaller patch? Brighter or dimmer?'
experiments.observe: The straight beam makes a small, bright circle. The slanting beam makes a bigger, dimmer oval covering more squares.
experiments.why: The same amount of light spread over more squares gives less light, and less warmth, to each square. When our half of the Earth leans towards the Sun, sunlight hits us more directly and the days are longer, so it is summer. When it leans away, the light comes at a slant and the days are shorter: winter. Distance from the Sun is not the cause.
experiments.safety: Do not shine the torch into anyone's eyes.

activities.title: The planet walk
need: big steps (each about 1 metre), or a measuring tape
a football (Sun), a rava grain (Mercury), a mustard seed (Venus), a mustard seed (Earth), a rava grain (Mars), a marble (Jupiter), a slightly smaller marble (Saturn), two chana (Uranus, Neptune)
steps: Put the football 'Sun' at the start. Put each planet on a paper label so it does not get lost.

Walk and place each planet this many big steps from the Sun: Mercury 10, Venus 19, Earth 26, Mars 40, Jupiter 135, Saturn 250, Uranus 500, Neptune 780. If you run out of space, stop at Jupiter. Point out that Neptune would be more than half a kilometre away.

In a flat, make it ten times smaller. A small lime is the Sun, and each planet is a speck of dust. Then Earth is 2 and a half big steps from the Sun, Mars 4, Jupiter 14 (try the building corridor) and Neptune about 80.

At each planet, say one fact: Venus is the hottest planet. Mars is red with rusty dust. Saturn has rings. Neptune is blue and very windy. Then stand at Earth and look back at the Sun. Ask: 'Is space crowded or empty?'
activities.outcome: Your child sees that the planets are tiny and the solar system is almost all empty space. The rocky planets are close to the Sun and the giants are far away.

activities.title: Saptarishi star viewer
steps: Copy the seven stars of the Saptarishi (a ladle of four stars and a handle of three) onto the bottom of the cup.
With help, poke a pinhole at each star.
In a dark room, put the torch inside the cup and shine it on the ceiling.
Add Dhruva Tara as a separate hole, beyond the two 'pointer' stars at the front of the ladle's bowl.
activities.outcome: A ceiling star pattern that helps your child find the real Saptarishi and the Pole Star.

project.title: My sky book
steps: Fold three A4 sheets into a little book.
Page 1: what I saw in the sky at dusk.
Page 2: things that make light and things that reflect it.
Page 3: the planets in order, with a drawing of the planet walk.
Page 4: Moon drawings with dates, and the four shapes from the ball-and-lamp test.
Page 5: the Saptarishi and Dhruva Tara.
Page 6: drawings of the Earth's spin, its journey round the Sun, and its tilt.
project.outcome: A home-made sky book your child uses to teach the family what is in the sky and why.

game.title: Star, Planet or Moon?
rules: Cut out the cards and shuffle the clue cards. Put the three category cards face up.
Turn over a clue card and read it aloud.
The first to point to the right category card and give a reason wins the card.
If there is an argument, check the back of the card.
Most cards at the end wins.

PLANET
MOON

I am red with rusty dust.
I go round the Earth about once a month.

Galileo saw four of us going round Jupiter.

big: If the stars are suns, could some of them have planets with someone looking back at us?
Do the star patterns belong to the stars or to the people who named them?
Why do you think almost every culture in the world has stories about the Moon?
Is a dark night sky something worth protecting? Who should decide?

challenge.q: 'It is hot in summer because the Earth is closer to the Sun.' Is it?
challenge.hint: No. The Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, when it is winter in India. Seasons come from the Earth's tilt. When our half leans towards the Sun, sunlight is more direct and days are longer. Ask: if distance were the reason, why would Australia have summer in December?

challenge.q: 'The Moon only comes out at night.' Does it?
challenge.hint: The Moon is up in the daytime for about half the month. Look for it in the morning in the days after Purnima, or in the afternoon in the days before. It is pale because the sky is so bright.

challenge.q: 'Stars twinkle because they flicker on and off.' Do they?
challenge.hint: Stars shine steadily. They twinkle because their light passes through our moving air on the way to us. Astronauts in space see stars shining without a twinkle. Ask: would stars twinkle more or less above a high mountain, where the air is still and thin?

perspectives.view: A dung beetle rolls a ball of dung to eat, and must roll it away quickly in a straight line before other beetles steal it. In 2013 scientists in South Africa showed that at night some dung beetles keep their line straight by steering with the glowing band of the Milky Way. Ask: who else might need a dark sky that we never think about?

perspectives.who: Kerala farmers and the Njattuvela calendar
perspectives.view: Farmers in Kerala have long timed their sowing and planting by Njattuvela. These are periods of about two weeks, each named after the star group (nakshatra) the Sun is passing through, like Thiruvathira. Ask: why might farmers watch the sky as carefully as scientists?

Navigators from Pacific islands crossed thousands of kilometres of open ocean by watching where stars rise and set, without maps or compasses. In 1976 the canoe Hōkūleʻa sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti this way, guided by Mau Piailug, a navigator from the island of Satawal. Ask: whose knowledge of the sky gets written in school books, and whose does not?

voices.who: The International Astronomical Union (2006), and Alan Stern (born 1957), USA
voices.idea: In 2006 the astronomers of the International Astronomical Union voted that a planet must go round the Sun, be round, and have cleared its path of other objects. Pluto has not cleared its path, so it became a 'dwarf planet'.
voices.then: Many people were upset. Only a few hundred of the thousands of astronomers voted. Alan Stern, who led the New Horizons spacecraft that flew past Pluto in 2015, says the rule is wrong and Pluto is a planet.
voices.now: Most astronomers use the 2006 definition, but the argument is still alive. Pluto has mountains of ice, a thin air and maybe an ocean under its ice.
voices.ask: Should a planet be decided by what it is like (round, with mountains and air) or by where it is and what is around it? Which rule would you choose?

voices.idea: In 1609 and 1610 he pointed a telescope he had made himself at the sky. He saw mountains and craters on the Moon, and four moons going round Jupiter. This showed that not everything goes round the Earth.
voices.then: Many scholars and church leaders disagreed with his idea that the Earth moves round the Sun. In 1633 he was put on trial and kept under house arrest for the rest of his life.
voices.now: Everything Galileo saw is accepted. The four moons he found are called the Galilean moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.
voices.ask: Galileo said, in effect, 'Look through my telescope and see for yourself.' Why is 'see for yourself' such a powerful kind of evidence? Can it ever trick you?

voices.who: Cecilia Payne, later Payne-Gaposchkin (1900–1979), England and USA
voices.idea: In her 1925 PhD at Harvard she showed, by studying starlight, that stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium, not of the same mix as the Earth.
voices.then: The leading astronomer Henry Norris Russell told her the result was 'clearly impossible', and she wrote in her thesis that it was probably not real. A few years later Russell reached the same answer by another way, and was often given the credit.
voices.now: She was right: hydrogen and helium make up almost all of every star. She later became the first woman to be a full professor at Harvard, and to head a department there.
voices.ask: Cecilia Payne doubted her own result because a famous man said it was impossible. When should you trust your own evidence over an expert?

voices.idea: One of the women hired at Harvard College Observatory to study photographs of starlight for low pay, she sorted stars into types by the pattern of their light, in the order O, B, A, F, G, K, M, from hottest to coolest. She classified about 350,000 stars, more than anyone else in history, sometimes at a rate of three a minute.
voices.then: At first the work of these women was seen as mere 'computing' or cataloguing, and they were paid much less than men. Cannon, who was almost deaf from her twenties, became famous in her lifetime; in 1925 she was the first woman to receive an honorary doctorate from Oxford University.
voices.now: Her O-B-A-F-G-K-M system is still used by every astronomer. Our Sun is a G star.
voices.ask: Sorting looks like a boring job. How can careful sorting lead to a big discovery? Can you think of something you could sort at home that might show a pattern?

check.q: Is the Sun a star? Why does it look so much bigger than other stars?
check.a: Yes. It looks bigger and brighter because it is much nearer to us than any other star.

check.q: What is the difference between a star and a planet?
check.a: A star makes its own light. A planet goes round a star and shines only by reflecting its light.

check.q: Name the planets in order from the Sun.
check.a: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.

check.q: Why does the Moon seem to change shape?
check.a: Half the Moon is always lit by the Sun. As it goes round the Earth we see different amounts of the lit half.
The Earth spins on its axis once about every 24 hours; the side facing the Sun has day.
The time the Earth takes to go once round the Sun, about 365 days.
Because the Earth is tilted. When our half leans towards the Sun, sunlight is more direct and days are longer (summer); when it leans away, it is winter.

check.q: How do you find the Pole Star?
check.a: Follow the two pointer stars at the end of the Saptarishi's ladle.

story.title: The Firefly Who Wanted to Be a Star
text: In the hills above the village of Purushwadi, where the forest smells of wet earth and wild mango just before the rains, there lived a young firefly called Tara. She had grown her wings only a few nights before, and everything was new to her: the cool leaves, the croak of frogs, the soft light that pulsed in her own belly whenever she felt happy.
On her first night out, she flew to the top of a fern and looked up. And there, across the whole black sky, were thousands and thousands of lights.
"Oh," said Tara. "Look at all the fireflies!"

They were much smaller than the fireflies around her, and they did not blink the way fireflies blink, on and off, on and off. They shone steadily, only trembling a little, as if they were shy. "They must be the oldest fireflies," Tara decided, "the ones who have flown highest of all. One day I will fly up there and join them."

The other fireflies laughed at her. They were busy with their own blinking, flashing their lights in rhythm until the whole valley pulsed like a heart. "Nobody has ever reached the high ones," said an old firefly. "Don't waste your nights."

But Tara had decided. The next night she began to climb. She flew up past the karvi bushes, up past the bamboo, up and up the trunk of the tallest jamun tree on the hill. Her wings ached. The air grew colder. At last she reached the very top leaf, and she clung to it, panting, her little light flickering.
She looked up. The high fireflies were exactly as small as before. Not one bit bigger. Not one bit nearer.
Tara felt something sink inside her. She had flown higher than any firefly she knew, and she had come no closer at all.

Far away, on the opposite hill, a tiny light was bobbing. It was small, and a little yellow, and it did not blink. "Another high one," Tara thought, "come down to look for me." She watched it move slowly through the dark, down the hill, across the stream, and up the path towards her tree.

As it came, it grew. It grew from a pinprick into a spark, and from a spark into a glow, and from a glow into a blazing white circle that lit up the leaves and the bark and the whole tree, so bright she had to turn her face away. Voices came with it.
"Switch it off, Anu, you'll scare them!"

The light clicked out. Below the jamun tree stood a girl and her mother, holding a torch. They had come up from the city to see the fireflies, the way many people do in the weeks before the monsoon. They sat down quietly in the grass and waited for their eyes to get used to the dark.
Tara sat very still on her leaf. The torch had been a tiny dot on the far hill. Up close, it had been a great blazing sun. It was the same torch. Only the distance had changed.

She looked up at the high ones again, and for the first time she felt a shiver that was not from the cold. If the torch had looked so small from so far away, how far away must the high ones be? And how big, really, and how bright?
"Amma," whispered the girl below, "are stars like fireflies?"

"In a way," said her mother. "They make their own light, like fireflies. But each star is a sun, a huge ball of glowing gas, much bigger than the whole Earth. They're just very, very far away. Our Sun is a star too. It's just the one we live next to."
"So somewhere far away," said the girl, "someone could be looking at our Sun, and it looks like a tiny dot to them."
"Maybe," said her mother. "Nobody knows yet."

Tara did not understand all the words. But she understood the torch. The high ones were not fireflies who had flown far. They were suns bigger than the world, so far away that even the tallest tree was no nearer to them than the ground. And the great hot light that came up every morning and sent the fireflies to sleep under the leaves, that too was one of them. The nearest one.
She could never reach them. She knew that now. It should have made her sad, but it didn't. It made her feel small in a way that was somehow wonderful, like being a tiny boat on a very big sea.

Down in the valley, the other fireflies had started their blinking again, all together, on and off, on and off, a whole forest of tiny lights calling to each other in the dark. Tara let go of the leaf. She drifted down, down through the cool air, down past the girl and her mother, who gasped and pointed, down into the bright, pulsing crowd of her own people.
And there, with her small near light, among all the other small near lights, she began to blink.
story.epiphany: Stars are suns. They look tiny only because they are very far away, and the Sun is simply the nearest star. The turn is the torch: a pinprick on the far hill and a blazing light up close, the same torch at a different distance. Tara also learns that stars make their own light, like fireflies, and she finds her place among her own kind.
ask: Why did the 'high ones' look no bigger when Tara reached the top of the tree?
What did the torch teach Tara?
Why does the girl's mother say our Sun is a star?
Could someone on a far planet see our Sun? What would it look like to them?
At the end, why do you think Tara went back down?

ideas.idea: The Sun is a star, and every star is a sun.
ideas.more: The near torch and the far torch show it: the same light looks tiny when it is far away. The nearest star after the Sun is so far that its light takes over four years to reach us.

ideas.idea: Space is mostly empty, and we are very small in it.
ideas.more: In the planet walk, the Sun is a football, the Earth is a mustard seed 26 big steps away, and Neptune is more than half a kilometre away. Between them is almost nothing.

ideas.idea: Three movements of the Earth give us day, year and seasons.
ideas.more: The Earth's spin gives day and night. Its journey round the Sun gives the year. Its tilt gives the seasons. The Moon's journey round us gives the month, and the word 'month' comes from 'Moon'.

unknowns: Is there life on any other planet? Scientists have found thousands of planets round other stars, but nobody knows yet whether anything lives on them.
Nobody knows how big the whole universe is, or whether it has an edge.
Pluto has mountains and maybe a hidden ocean. Why a small, cold world is so active is still a puzzle.
